varieties.name: Watsoniana
varieties.note: Sold under this name, and usually a form of Alocasia longiloba. Dark corrugated leaf with bone-white veins, from the forest floor of Borneo and Sumatra. Slow even when happy, and the first to sulk when the air dries or the night turns cold.

varieties.name: Amazonica (Polly)
varieties.note: The common hybrid, arrow-shaped with pale veins and a wavy edge. Not from the Amazon. Hardier than most of the genus indoors, and the one that most often drops every leaf and comes back from the corm.

varieties.name: Zebrina
varieties.note: Grown as much for the banded stems as the leaves. Wants the brightest light in this profile's range; in a dim corner the stems stretch and the plant leans.

varieties.name: Frydek
varieties.note: Velvet green with white veins. The velvet leaves mark with water and dislike being wiped, so water the soil and let the air do the rest.

varieties.name: Cuprea
varieties.note: Thick metallic leaf, small and slow. Needs the highest humidity of these and resents a draught more than it resents a dim week.

varieties.name: Macrorrhiza
varieties.note: The giant. Takes more light and more water than the rest of the genus and outgrows a windowsill quickly; these ranges are set for the smaller kinds.

watering.label: Water well, then let the top third dry before the next. The corm rots in standing wet

drainage.label: Chunky aroid mix, bark and perlite. Water should run through, not sit

young: Too dark for a young plant. A two-leaf nursery plant has no reserve to spend and simply stops.
Dim. The next leaf comes up smaller than the one before it, which is how this genus fades out.
A little short for a young plant. It keeps the leaves it has and makes no more.
established: Too dark. Leaf stalks stretch and lean, and the plant carries fewer leaves at a time.
Dim. New growth is smaller each round and the veining loses its contrast.
A little short. It holds, but it will not add a leaf.

young: Too much for a young plant. The newest leaf pales between its veins.
Well past what a young plant takes. New leaves crisp at the edge as they open.
Far too much for a young plant. Thin new leaves bleach and crisp in a single afternoon.
established: Burning. Pale patches spread between the veins and do not recover.
Too much. The leaf yellows overall and the edges go papery.
Far too much. These grow under a canopy; direct midday sun scorches them through.
